papers.title: Rapid antidepressant effects of psilocybin without increased SV2A binding: baseline binding predicts response
papers.abstract: We report a pre-registered [11C]UCB-J PET sub-study of a recently published randomized trial in which a single psilocybin dose produced rapid and sustained antidepressant effects in major depressive disorder (MDD). Synaptic loss has been implicated in MDD, and psychedelics induce synaptic remodeling in preclinical models within 24 hours, raising the possibility that psilocybin's antidepressant effects involve increased synaptic density. We used the PET radioligand [11C]UCB-J targeting synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) to test this in thirty-five participants with moderate-to-severe recurrent MDD randomized 1:1 to a single dose of 25 mg psilocybin or 100 mg niacin placebo, both with psychotherapeutic support. [11C]UCB-J PET was performed 2-7 days before and 15 (+/-7) days after dosing. Despite significant clinical improvement in the psilocybin group, we found no evidence of a group-level increase in SV2A binding (VT or BPND) relative to niacin in the hippocampus or frontal cortex. In secondary analyses, higher baseline VT was associated with greater subsequent clinical improvement in the psilocybin group; this survived FDR correction at Day 8 and Day 15 (two of three pre-registered timepoints). Change in VT was associated with greater subsequent clinical improvement in unadjusted analyses, but these associations were attenuated after adjustment for baseline VT and baseline MADRS and did not survive FDR correction. These findings indicate that substantial antidepressant improvement after psilocybin can occur without a detectable group-level increase in SV2A binding, while raising the possibility that baseline SV2A binding could help identify individuals more likely to respond.

papers.title: Co-production of an oral health intervention: Enabling Service Users with Severe Mental Illness to Learn about and Engage (SMILE) with Good Oral Health
papers.abstract: Background: People with severe mental illness (SMI) experience poorer oral health than the general population. They are less likely to visit the dentist or brush their teeth and face unique barriers to accessing oral health support. There is a limited number of oral health interventions for people with SMI, and there is no conclusive evidence on their effectiveness. An integrated oral health intervention delivered by mental health professionals in a community mental healthcare setting could offer a scalable option to oral health support for people with SMI. In this paper we report on the process of co-producing such an intervention in England. Methods: The intervention development process was informed by Hawkins co-production framework. In this paper we report on stages 2 (co-production) and 3 (prototyping). Two online and two face-to-face co-production workshops took place (N=22) involving service users with SMI (n=6), mental health professionals (n=8) and dental health professionals (n=8). Two online patient and public involvement consultations, and a professional stakeholder meeting were held during the co-production process to provide feedback on the co-production process. The workshops informed the core components, format and content of the intervention. Results: The co-production process resulted in five intervention components: 1) Initiating a conversation about oral health, 2) providing advice to people with SMI on keeping their teeth and mouth healthy, 3) weekly tooth brushing text reminders, and 4) mental health professionals updating the care record to document the administration of this intervention. To support intervention delivery, we co-produced an intervention flowchart, an intervention leaflet for people with SMI, and a training manual for mental health professionals delivering the intervention. Conclusion: We co-produced an integrated oral health intervention to be delivered to service users with SMI in community mental health settings. The next stage of the research is a single-arm feasibility study to assess whether the intervention is acceptable to people with SMI and feasible to deliver within the NHS.

papers.title: Greater Stress Response Network (SRN) Connectivity is Associated with Higher Worry in Men and Women Especially in Later Life
papers.abstract: Background: Late-life anxiety is common and disabling, with pathological worry as a core feature. The Stress Response Network (SRN: amygdala, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, paraventricular nucleus), which modulates threat and stress reactivity, and its interaction with the Executive Control Network (ECN), anchored by the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which supports emotional regulation via top-down cognitive control, may underlie individual differences in worry severity. We hypothesize higher SRN connectivity to be associated with greater worry severity and that this relationship may be moderated positively by older age, and female sex. Methods: We recruited older adults with varying worry. Resting-state fMRI was used to compute SRN connectivity and SRN-ECN connectivity. Regression models tested associations between connectivity and worry (PSWQ), anxiety (HARS), and rumination (RSQ), adjusting for age, sex, race, and education. Exploratory models examined age and sex moderation and associations with emotion regulation/suppression and cognitive function. Results: Among 131 participants who were [≥] 50 years old, with varying levels of worry severity, SRN connectivity was significantly associated with greater worry severity (B=23.51 (SE = 12.12), p<0.05), whereas SRN-ECN connectivity was not. SRN connectivity was lower with greater age (B=-0.003 (SE=0.001), p=0.04), yet older individuals reported greater worry than younger with comparable connectivity. Greater language domain cognitive function was associated with lower SRN connectivity but higher SRN-ECN connectivity, while greater overall cognitive function was associated with lower SRN-ECN connectivity. Women reported lower use of daily expressive suppression and higher performance across cognitive measures than men. Higher daily use of expressive suppression was not significantly associated with either connectivity measure. Discussion: SRN connectivity, rather than SRN-ECN connectivity, may serve as the primary neural correlate of worry, shaped by age and cognitive function.

papers.title: The cognitive profile of the schizophrenia-associated 3q29 deletion syndrome and the reciprocal 3q29 duplication syndrome
papers.abstract: 3q29 deletion syndrome (3q29del) and the reciprocal 3q29 duplication syndrome (3q29dup) are associated with a range of neuropsychiatric phenotypes, including impaired cognition. However, previous sample sizes have been small, and cognitive performance has not been systematically compared between 3q29del and 3q29dup. For both disorders, the impact of familial background on cognition is unknown. 3q29del is associated with high risk for schizophrenia; in the general population individuals at Clinical High Risk (CHR) for psychosis exhibit impaired cognition, but the relationship between CHR status and cognition in 3q29del is unexplored. Here we address these questions in the largest sample of 3q29del and 3q29dup ever evaluated. Individuals with 3q29del (n=103, 58.3% male), 3q29dup (n=38, 55.3% male), and controls (n=54, 42.6% male) were assessed with the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, 5th Edition (PPVT-5) and the Penn Computerized Neurocognitive Battery (Penn-CNB). Total PPVT-5 scores and global, domain-level, and task-level Penn-CNB scores were compared across groups. Compared to controls, 3q29del participants scored an average of 24.6 and 22.9 points lower on the PPVT and Penn CNB, respectively (p<3E-16); 3q29dup participants scored an average of 18.8 and 14.2 points lower on the PPVT and Penn CNB (p<4E-6). In addition, 3q29del and 3q29dup exhibit unique profiles of cognitive deficits. To assess the impact of familial background on cognition, we evaluated unaffected relatives of 3q29del (n=140, 38.6% male), 3q29dup (n=25, 24.0% male), and controls (n=45, 11.1% male). The average familial shift on the Penn-CNB was 22.4 points for 3q29del and 16.7 points for 3q29 dup. Individuals with 3q29del+CHR exhibited greater cognitive deficits than 3q29del-CHR. These results demonstrate that both 3q29del and 3q29dup are associated with significant cognitive impairment and indicate that cognitive testing should be standard of care for individuals diagnosed with 3q29del or 3q29dup.

papers.title: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Brief Health Chatbot Acceptability Scale (CAS): A Pilot Study
papers.abstract: Background. Conversational agents (chatbots) are increasingly used to deliver health information to middle-aged and older adults, a population in which the determinants of technology acceptance are known to diverge from those of younger users. However, acceptability is inconsistently defined and typically measured with ad hoc, unvalidated instruments. The psychometrically sound chatbot measures that exist assess usability rather than acceptability or were validated in student samples. Objective. To develop and conduct an initial psychometric evaluation of a brief, 10-item health chatbot acceptance measure grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB). Methods. Twenty adults (mean age = 52.8 years, range 28-81; 85% aged 40 or older; 75% female) enrolled in a sleep-application pilot usability study completed the 10 candidate items, the System Usability Scale (SUS), and sleep measures (PROMIS Sleep Disturbance 8a; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). We examined item performance, internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha), dimensionality (exploratory factor analysis with oblique rotation), and convergent validity (correlations with the SUS). Results. A two-factor structure emerged and was invariant across rotation methods, resulting in an Information Quality factor and an Acceptance factor (interfactor r = .39). All items loaded [≥] .60 on their primary factor; mean communality was .83. Subscale reliabilities were high (Information Quality = .96; Acceptance = .94; full scale = .93). Both subscales correlated with the SUS in the expected direction (r = .69 and r = .59), providing preliminary support for convergent validity. Conclusions. The measure shows a coherent and theory-consistent two-factor structure and shows preliminary evidence of reliability and convergent validity. Given the small pilot sample, these results must be viewed as provisional but identify the measure as a candidate for formal validation in a larger, independent sample.

papers.title: Classical machine learning versus transformers for predicting daily psychological distress from passive smartphone sensing and self-report: a prospective cohort study
papers.abstract: Objective: We test whether data collected from daily passive smartphone sensing and self-reports can predict daily significant psychological distress with meaningful potential clinical utility, comparing across best-in-class machine learning algorithms. Methods: In this prospective cohort study, 169 community-dwelling adults completed baseline surveys followed by 7 days of passive smartphone sensing (accelerometer, GPS, power state) and end-of-day Brief Symptom Inventory-18 (BSI-18) assessments. Cases were defined as days (total n = 1,062) where participants' psychological distress measured with the sex-specific BSI-18 Global Severity Index T-score was [≥]63 (prevalence 11.2%). Four classical models (artificial neural network, elastic net, support vector machine [SVM], extreme gradient boosting [XGB]) and four transformers (sensor-only or multimodal; standard or fusion architecture) were tuned, Platt-calibrated and evaluated on held-out participants (210 records, 25 cases) with participant-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results: The SVM (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.84; 95% CI 0.71-0.93), the multimodal fusion transformer (0.84; 0.69-0.95) and XGB (0.82; 0.63-0.94) discriminated best; sensor-only transformers performed at chance (0.49-0.50). At the default threshold of 0.50, elastic net logistic regression was the best classifier (sensitivity 0.56, positive predictive value 0.64). At 0.12 (near the outcome prevalence), the SVM detected all cases (negative predictive value 1.00), but positive predictive values were low for all models (0.13-0.26). Decision-curve analysis favored most models over treat-all and treat-none lines at thresholds between 0.05 and 0.25. Baseline survey items, mainly on functional impairment, had the largest feature importance. Conclusions: Compact classical models performed as well as transformers, which were considerably more computationally intensive. Decision-curve analysis supports further clinical exploration of these tools for triaging daily psychological distress, though our results suggest the relative value of psychosocial assessments and digital data should be carefully analyzed. External validation is needed before clinical use.

papers.title: Greater than the sum of its parts: A novel psychiatric multimorbidity metric applied to rare disease
papers.abstract: Importance: Rare genetic syndromes are often drivers of complex multimorbidity. However, current methods consider multimorbidity as the sum of chronic diagnoses, which does not account for subthreshold impairment. Objective: To develop a quantitative multimorbidity score (MMS) for rare genetic syndromes that summarizes the neurodevelopmental and psychiatric multimorbidity landscape, including subthreshold symptoms, using 3q29 deletion and 3q29 duplication syndromes as hallmark examples. Design: We developed a multimorbidity metric and applied it to cross-sectional data. Remote phenotyping from 2023-2026. In-person phenotyping from 2017-2020. Setting: Remote phenotyping conducted at Rutgers University. In-person phenotyping conducted at Emory University. Participants: Participants were 6 years of age and older. 3q29del and 3q29dup recruited from the 3q29 registry and direct referrals and contacts. Syndrome status confirmed by genetic report review. Typically developing controls recruited from community sources and ResearchMatch. Main Outcomes and Measures: We developed a quantitative MMS across five distinct domains of functioning, operationalized as the sum of z-scores across six standardized assessments. The MMS was calculated for each study participant and compared across groups. Within 3q29del, we evaluated the relationship between MMSs and Vineland-3 adaptive behavior. Results: 96 individuals with 3q29del (52.08% male, 18.01+/-11.47 years old), 28 individuals with 3q29dup (50.00% male, 20.82+/-13.64 years old), and 53 controls (41.51% male, 17.77+/-10.74 years old) were included. 3q29del and 3q29dup participants had significantly lower MMS scores compared to controls (3q29del mean=-8.22+/-4.67, 3q29dup mean=-6.47+/-4.66, control mean=1.36+/-2.35, 3q29del p<2E-16, 3q29dup p=4.89E-16). Within 3q29del, subjects with more severe multimorbidity had greater impairment in adaptive behavior (R2=0.589, p<2E-16). The quantitative MMS is more highly correlated with adaptive behavior than traditional diagnosis-based multimorbidity metrics (quantitative MMS R2=0.589, diagnosis-based multimorbidity R2=0.447). In a subset of 24 3q29del participants with longitudinal data (58.33% male, 13.17+/-9.08 years old at first evaluation, average time to follow up=5.17+/-0.87 years), the MMS is stable over time (R2=0.858, p=8.34E-8). Conclusions and Relevance: Our novel quantitative MMS is an improved metric for measuring psychiatric multimorbidity in high-risk populations, and accounts for the impact of subthreshold impairments. When applied to 3q29del and 3q29dup, it quantifies the individual burden of multimorbidity, is stable over time, and is associated with clinical outcome measures.

papers.title: Transdiagnostic Functional Brain Alterations Across Familial and Phenotypic Risk Samples: A Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: Importance: Psychiatric risk factors are often associated with multiple clinical outcomes. However, it remains unclear whether functional brain activation changes are shared across risk for mood, anxiety, and psychotic disorders. Objective: To determine which patterns of functional brain activation are shared across risk for different psychiatric disorders, defined using phenotypic (e.g., clinical) and familial risk paradigms, relative to control samples. Data Sources: PubMed and Web of Science were searched for task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies involving samples at risk for a mood, anxiety, or psychotic disorder, published between January 2000 and July 2026. Study Selection: Studies published in English, with whole brain results, comparing a high-risk sample to a control sample, with a mean age of 30 years or less, were included. Of the 5,748 studies screened, 101 met selection criteria. Data Extraction and Synthesis: Peak voxel coordinates from contrasts were extracted. Study quality was assessed using an adapted neuroimaging methods quality checklist. Peak coordinates were pooled within studies, and a random effects activation likelihood estimation meta-analysis was conducted using the Python package JALE. Main Outcomes and Measures: Statistical maps of spatial convergence in task-related brain activation were computed across risk groups and within subgroups defined by disorder risk (mood, anxiety, or psychotic disorder risk), ascertainment paradigm (phenotypic, familial), and task domain (cognitive, affective, reward). Statistical significance was assessed using permutation-based cluster-level family-wise error (cFWE) correction. Results: The studies included comprised 2534 high-risk participants and 2686 controls. Across psychosis, mood, and anxiety risk groups, there was a common area of functional activation in the left lateral prefrontal cortex (k = 319, p < 0.05 cFWE), reflecting greater activation in high-risk groups compared to controls. Approximately 30% of studies in each risk group contributed to this finding, reflecting both ascertainment paradigms and all three task types. Within the psychosis risk group, additional alterations were identified in the orbitofrontal cortex and anterior insula. Conclusions and Relevance: Increased left lateral prefrontal activation was shared across risk groups despite methodological heterogeneity. Because this region supports higher-order executive functioning and undergoes prolonged maturation, this finding may represent a shared marker of vulnerability across psychiatric risk groups.

papers.title: Beyond Perinatal Mood: Breadth of Psychiatric Symptoms and Delay Discounting as Correlates of Mothers' Relational Reports from Pregnancy Through Adult Children
papers.abstract: Maternal mental illness affects roughly one in five mothers in the United States, yet most evidence linking it to the mother-child relationship comes from the first postpartum year and relies on self-report measures of depression, anxiety, and stress. In 613 women spanning five family contexts - pregnancy and mothers whose youngest child was aged 0-2, 3-12, 13-17, or 18 and older - we examined twelve psychological constructs as correlates of mothers' relational reports. Eleven were associated with relational reports individually; entered together, only three retained independent associations surviving false discovery rate correction: cross-domain psychiatric symptom burden (beta = 0.38), delay discounting (beta = -0.11), and orienting sensitivity (beta = 0.10). To our knowledge, this is the first peer-reviewed study linking delay discounting to maternal relational reports. Depression, anxiety, anger, perceived stress, and negative affect fell to non-significance, and the symptom composite that displaced them contains none of those domains, indicating that breadth of psychiatric symptoms, not their type, tracked relational reports. A person-centered analysis converged: the latent profile with the poorest relational reports was defined by symptoms across multiple domains rather than by elevated stress alone. Associations varied across family contexts, though because each context used a different relational instrument, differences cannot be attributed to child age. These cross-sectional findings suggest that the psychological dimension most closely tied to maternal relational reports is broader than the perinatal mood constructs around which research and screening are organized, and that cross-domain symptom assessment warrants prospective evaluation as a complement to mood screening.

papers.title: The Feasibility, Acceptability, and Perceived Need for Suicide Initiatives for Children in UK Primary Schools
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Currently, there are no specific suicide prevention programmes for primary (elementary) schools within the UK. However, given the rise in suicidal thoughts and/or behaviours amongst children under 11 years, the feasibility, acceptability, and perceived need for these programmes need to be assessed. Aims: This qualitative scoping study aimed to explore whether there is a perceived need for suicide prevention programmes in primary schools and, if so, what these should look like. Sample(s) & Methods: 92 participants took part in the study. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with mental health professionals (N= 22), school staff (N= 8), and parents of children who had experienced suicidal ideation, behaviours, or been bereaved by suicide (N=7). Focus groups were conducted with secondary school students (N= 36) and primary school students (N= 19) across 5 schools. Data were analysed using thematic framework analysis. Results: Three main themes were identified: 1) the necessity of suicide prevention programmes for primary schools, 2) barriers affecting delivery and potential solutions, 3) the transition period from primary to secondary school. Conclusion: Overall, participants supported the need and acceptability of suicide prevention programmes for primary schools, particularly due to the rising concerns about suicidality among younger children and evidence that suicide-related discussions are already occurring within peer groups. However, careful consideration needs to be given to ensure it is delivered in a safe and age-appropriate way, with a focus on dispelling myths, promoting help seeking, and increasing knowledge.

papers.title: Anticholinergic Medications and Health in Adults with Autism or Intellectual Disability
papers.abstract: Objective: Contributors to autistic adults' elevated risk for negative aging-related outcomes, including Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD), falls, and mortality remain underexplored. One candidate factor is exposure to medications with anticholinergic (AC) effects. Thus, this study assessed prevalence of medications with AC effects, and their associations with ADRD, falls, and mortality across four groups: autism-only, autism+intellectual disability (ID), ID-only, and controls. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 2017-2019 US linked Medicare and Medicaid claims data for 40+ year-olds. Autism, ID, ADRD, and falls were identified using validated algorithms, and mortality was based on Medicare/Medicaid death indicators. Medications were coded using a comprehensive AC potency scale. AC medication exposure effects and interactions between AC potency and group were examined using modified Poisson regressions. Sensitivity analyses to address indication bias excluded persons prescribed antidepressant and/or antipsychotic medication(s). Results: All three clinical groups experienced significantly greater AC medication exposure (autism+ID: 92.5%>ID-only: 88.6%>autism-only: 80.0%) than non-autistic/non-ID controls (61.3%). Additionally, AC medications were more frequently associated with ADRD, falls, and mortality in all of these groups. Stepwise associations between AC potency levels and ADRD, falls, and mortality were found, and these effects were more prominent for persons with autism and/or ID relative to the control sample. Interpretation: This study provides a foundational examination of exposure to AC medication effects and their associations with aging-related outcomes in middle-age and older autistic adults and adults with ID. AC medication exposure represents one potential modifiable risk factor for negative aging-related outcomes in these groups.

papers.title: Feeling Too Much or Too Little: Alexithymia Moderates How Self-Reported Physiological Hyperarousal Shapes Risky Decisions
papers.abstract: Background: Embodied cognition frameworks propose that physiological states shape decision-making, yet the contribution of sustained threat-related hyperarousal and individual differences in interoceptive integration remains poorly understood. This study examined whether self-reported physiological hyperarousal predicted Prospect Theory decision parameters: loss aversion, value sensitivity, and choice consistency; and whether alexithymia moderated these associations. Methods: Sixty-eight healthy young adults (M age = 18.94, SD = 1.46; 85% women) completed the DASS-21 anxiety subscale as a measure of hyperarousal, the TAS-20 as a measure of alexithymia, and a 64-trial Mixed Gambles Task; individual Prospect Theory parameters were estimated via hierarchical Bayesian analysis. Moderation analyses were conducted using Hayes' PROCESS macro with Johnson-Neyman probing. Results: Self-reported hyperarousal negatively predicted choice consistency and value sensitivity, but not loss aversion. Alexithymia moderated both effects through distinct conditional patterns: the self-reported hyperarousal-choice consistency association was significant only below a TAS-20 threshold of 51.05 (67.65% of the sample), reflecting monotonic buffering; the self-reported hyperarousal value sensitivity association was significant within a bounded TAS-20 range (45.31-66.08), suggesting that intermediate alexithymia constitutes a zone of maximal vulnerability, though this model only reached trend significance and should be treated as exploratory. No effects emerged for loss aversion. Conclusion: These findings indicate that sustained hyperarousal could selectively degrade evaluative precision and decision consistency, while leaving loss aversion intact. Alexithymia may operate as a stage-specific, conditional moderator of the body-decision relationship.

papers.title: Peripheral immune biomarkers, brain imaging phenotypes and treatment response in major depressive disorder
papers.abstract: Immune dysregulation is implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), but its links to clinical features and in vivo brain phenotypes remain uncertain. We examined ten plasma biomarkers in 36 unmedicated MDD patients and 48 control participants using high-sensitivity immune profiling at baseline, alongside PET/MR imaging of brain serotonin transporter (SERT) binding and regional structural measures. Patients underwent three months of antidepressant treatment and were followed up with MR imaging. Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) was higher in MDD patients ({beta} = 0.66, 95% CI 0.22 - 1.11), and interleukin-33 (IL-33) correlated with subcortical volumes across all participants ({beta} = 0.22, 95% CI 0.07 - 0.38). No marker correlated with SERT binding or cortical thickness after correction, and neither SERT binding nor brain structural measures differed by diagnosis. In the longitudinal analysis, interleukin-13 (IL-13) was associated with greater antidepressant response during first-line treatment with escitalopram ({beta} = 1.09, 95% CI 0.56 - 1.61). IL-15 and IL-13 showed nominal associations with hippocampal volume increase after treatment. These findings support astroglial involvement in MDD and link peripheral immune variation to subcortical brain structure. IL-13 is a candidate prognostic marker of response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Its tentative association with longitudinal changes in hippocampal volume suggests that immune processes in MDD may be related to both the capacity for clinical improvement and brain structural plasticity during treatment.

papers.title: Modulating Amygdala Responses in Major Depressive Disorder using Naturalistic Neurofeedback with Emotional Faces
papers.abstract: Emotion regulation is critical to mental health, and its disruption can lead to psychiatric conditions such as major depressive disorder (MDD). MDD encompasses diverse symptoms, including anhedonia and anxiety, which may be associated with distinct patterns of altered neural activity. Interventions that address the neural mechanisms underlying these symptom dimensions may improve treatment efficacy. We investigated an adaptive, naturalistic real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging neurofeedback paradigm designed to differentially target anhedonia and anxiety through bidirectional amygdala regulation. Unlike conventional abstract feedback, our approach used emotional faces whose expressions changed dynamically according to ongoing amygdala activity, embedding neural self-regulation within a socially relevant emotional context. In this parallel-group study, 21 patients with MDD received one of two neurofeedback conditions. In the Happy-up group, patients attempted to increase amygdala activity by making a neutral face happier to enhance positive emotional responding. In the Fear-down group, patients attempted to decrease amygdala activity by making a fearful face less fearful to reduce negative emotional reactivity. Both groups showed the expected pattern of neural regulation during neurofeedback, with greater amygdala activity during Happy upregulation and decreasing amygdala activity during Fear downregulation. Following the intervention, patients showed reductions in depression severity, anxiety, and anhedonia, and more positive evaluations of neutral and happy faces. However, improvements in anhedonia and anxiety did not differ significantly between groups. These findings show bidirectional amygdala regulation through naturalistic neurofeedback in MDD. Although symptom-specific clinical effects were not established, the observed clinical improvements underscore the therapeutic potential of this approach.

papers.title: Nicotine and Cannabis Co-Use are Associated with Higher Symptom Burden than Use of Either Drug Alone in Early Psychosis: Results from a Multisite Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundDespite their high usage rates and associations with risk for psychosis and earlier age of symptom onset, few studies have examined relationships between nicotine and cannabis co-use and symptoms. Here we examined associations between symptom burden and cannabis/nicotine use/co-use in individuals with early psychosis (EP). MethodsThis cross-sectional, multisite cohort study used data from 738 individuals (mean age 22 years, 62% male) from the Early Psychosis Intervention Network (EPI-NET). Relationships between cannabis and/or nicotine use and frequency (over the prior 30 day period) and Modified Colorado Symptom Index (MCSI) scores were examined using mixed effects models, with site as a random factor and age, sex, and cannabis/nicotine use (none, nicotine only, cannabis only, or both) as fixed factors. Exploratory analyses also examined effects of frequency of use (daily vs. less than daily). Results59% of the sample used neither nicotine nor cannabis, 17% only nicotine, 9% only cannabis, and 16% both. Significant effects of use were observed on total MCSI score (F = 6.69, p < .001) driven by greater symptoms in individuals who used both cannabis and nicotine relative to neither, only nicotine, or only cannabis. More frequent use, furthermore, was associated with higher total score. ConclusionsThese results suggest that co-use of cannabis and nicotine is associated with greater symptom burden in EP, which may have implications for treatment strategies. Neuropharmacological mechanisms that may underlie this association are discussed.

papers.title: Capturing additional variance in impact of adolescent depression from free text: proof of concept and preliminary results
papers.abstract: Depression in adolescents has grown in prevalence in the past decade. Despite indications of differences in symptom presentation, measurement properties, and treatment response between adolescents and adults, research is dominated by adult participants. Qualitative work has identified symptomatic and functional domains important to depressed adolescents and those around them; however, there remains little quantitative evidence of how these domains relate to the functional impact of the disorder. In this preregistered study, we use adolescent self-report (n = 153) and parent-report (n = 106) responses in the depression section of the Development and Well-Being Assessment (DAWBA) to examine what information relevant to reported depression impact may be missing from its structured symptom-scale. We apply Large Language Models (LLMs) to participant free-text answers to extract information on a taxonomy of 80 outcomes. Through a sequential residual stacking framework that estimates incremental information in symptom sum-scores (S ), item-level symptom-scale answers (Q), and LLM-derived text representations (T ), we find that parent text contains information relevant to their report of depression impact that is not available in the structured symptom-scale, with the largest contributions concentrated in functioning-related domains (e.g., professional responsibilities, social exclusion, autonomy, coping). No such evidence was found in adolescent self-reports. Given the moderate sample size, these results are preliminary. Nonetheless, we provide a proof-of-concept framework for extracting information from open-ended free text in large existing datasets, and estimating incremental information across sources, which could be applied to uncover specific aspects of adolescent mental disorders across populations.

papers.title: Polydrug use and recreational motives are associated with lower posttraumatic symptoms in survivors of a mass trauma event
papers.abstract: ObjectiveDrug use after trauma is common, but polydrug use patterns, motives, and associations with subsequent symptoms are poorly understood. We examined these associations among mass-casualty terror attack survivors, 72% of whom used drugs immediately before trauma exposure. MethodsSurvivors of the October 7, 2023 Nova Festival attack reported use of six drug types (alcohol, cannabis, ketamine, stimulants, MDMA, psychedelics) and motives (avoidance, emotional regulation, self-medication, sleep, recreation) longitudinally at three timepoints (TP): 1-6 months (N=772), 8-12 months (N=453), and 17-24 months (N=302) post-attack. Separate latent class analyses of TP2 data characterized drug use, motives, and their combination. Linear regression and mixed-effects models examined associations between class membership and PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) scores, adjusting for age, sex, time since trauma, and TP1 PCL-5 scores. ResultsAt TP2, 70% reported polydrug use, 17% used one drug, and 13% reported no use. The high drug-load class (mean 4.6 drug types) had lower PCL-5 scores than the low drug-load class (mean 1.5 drug types); this difference was evident among participants using [≥]4 drug types and persisted through TP3. The self-medication-motive class had higher PCL-5 scores than the recreational-motive class. In joint analyses, recreational-motive users at both low and high drug loads had lower PCL-5 scores than participants reporting self-medication motives and primarily cannabis use. ConclusionsPolydrug use was common among the mass-trauma survivors in our study. Self-medication motives were associated with higher PTSD symptom severity than recreational motives. Unexpectedly, higher polydrug use was associated with lower PTSD symptom scores.

papers.title: Integrated Metabolomics Identifies Mitochondrial Dysfunction, Oxidative Membrane Remodeling, and Reduced Lipophilic Antioxidant Defenses in First-Episode Simple Dysmood Disorder
papers.abstract: BackgroundMetabolomic abnormalities in major depression have largely been investigated at the level of individual metabolites. We hypothesized that coordinated metabolic pathways, rather than isolated biomarkers, characterize first-episode simple dysmood disorder (FE-SDMD). MethodsUntargeted LC-MS metabolomics was performed in plasma from 44 FE-SDMD patients and 44 healthy controls. Differential metabolites were identified using Wilcoxon tests with false discovery rate correction and integrated with complementary machine-learning approaches. Curated metabolites were grouped into biologically informed functional modules, validated using principal component analysis, and examined in relation to clinical phenome dimensions, adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), and negative life events (NLEs). ResultsOf 450 detected metabolites, 298 remained significant after FDR correction and 240 additionally met fold-change criteria. Complementary feature-selection methods yielded a consensus panel of 20 biologically relevant metabolites that discriminated FE-SDMD from controls across multivariate and machine-learning analyses. Six functional modules revealed increased oxidative membrane remodeling, gut-liver dysfunction, mitochondrial bioenergetic dysfunction, reduced lipophilic antioxidant defenses and glucocorticoid metabolism, and altered dietary phytochemical metabolism. ACEs, particularly emotional neglect, and NLEs were associated with greater abnormalities across all modules. Gut-liver and mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, NLEs, and/or ACEs explained substantial variance in overall depression severity (66%), physiosomatic symptoms (41%), and suicidal ideation (43%). ConclusionsFunctional metabolic modules provide a biologically interpretable systems-biology framework linking metabolomic abnormalities, psychosocial adversity, and clinical phenotypes, supporting the neuroimmune-metabolic-oxidative (NIMETOX) model of depression.

papers.title: Decision-Making Under Stress, Biological Stress Responses, and Risk for Suicidal Behavior in Young Adults
papers.abstract: BackgroundStress may influence decision-making processes relevant to suicidal behavior, yet few studies have examined risky decision-making and expected value (EV) sensitivity under stress longitudinally among young adults at elevated suicide risk. MethodsParticipants included 233 young adults (18-30 years) with recent suicide attempts (n=55), suicidal ideation (n=59), psychiatric controls (n=71), and healthy controls (n=48). Hair cortisol concentration, circulating inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6, IL-10, IL-1ra, TNF-), Stressful Cups Task, and clinical measures were assessed at baseline, 3-, 6-, and 12-month follow-ups. ResultsParticipants with a history of suicide attempts showed greater reductions in risky choices under stress over time compared to healthy controls ({beta}=-0.119, p<0.001). Greater reductions in EV sensitivity under stress relative to neutral conditions predicted subsequent suicidal behavior (OR=0.530, 95% CI: 0.328-0.856, p=0.009). Higher C-reactive protein (CRP) was associated with fewer risky choices under both neutral ({beta} = -0.040, SE = 0.010, p < 0.001) and stress conditions ({beta} = -0.131, SE = 0.031, p < 0.001), while higher interleukin-6 (IL-6) was associated with fewer risky choices under neutral conditions ({beta} = -0.080, SE = 0.018, p < 0.001). Higher interleukin-10 (IL-10) was associated with greater reductions in risky choices under stress relative to neutral conditions over time ({beta} = -0.068, SE = 0.018, p < 0.001). No significant associations were observed for hair cortisol concentrations (HCC). ConclusionsStress-related changes in risky decision-making and reduced EV sensitivity may contribute to vulnerability to suicidal behavior. These findings highlight the importance of assessing decision-making under stress and examining inflammatory processes as potential mechanisms underlying suicide risk.

papers.title: Delayed-centrifugation blood collection tube for remote blood biomarker assessment
papers.abstract: IntroductionPlasma phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) and amyloid-{beta} 42 (A{beta}42) are advancing toward clinical use for Alzheimers disease (AD), but their reliability can be impacted by preanalytical handling. Although alternative collection tubes with distinct stabilization strategies--P100 (protease inhibitor) and HEMAcollect (hemolysis/platelet-activation minimization)--have been developed to stabilize plasma proteins, how well they preserve these markers remains unresolved; we therefore compared both against fresh standard EDTA tubes. MethodsIn 40 participants, plasma p-tau217 and A{beta}42 were measured (Lumipulse) in paired fresh EDTA, P100, and HEMAcollect samples after 5-day ambient storage. We assessed concentration change, rank-order preservation (Spearman {rho}), percentage difference, and diagnostic classification under the p-tau217/A{beta}42 ratio and p-tau217 alone. ResultsP100 preserved p-tau217 favorably, with high rank-order correlation ({rho}=0.98) and a modest median change (+12.1%), and its classification agreement with fresh EDTA reached 97.5% using p-tau217 alone. HEMAcollect showed greater p-tau217 signal loss (-57.5%). A{beta}42 was reduced in both tubes (-72.8% P100; -95.5% HEMAcollect) with loss of rank order, so neither preserved the p-tau217/A{beta}42 ratio. DiscussionStability was tube- and analyte-specific, and P100 consistently outperformed HEMAcollect--preserving p-tau217 rank order while HEMAcollect reduced signal across analytes. Although neither tube preserved the A{beta}42-dependent ratio, P100 shows potential for p-tau217-based workflows. Preanalytical stability must be established analyte by analyte before alternative tubes enter clinical AD diagnosis.

papers.title: Dyslexia extends beyond reading difficulties: genetic links with social functioning and well-being
papers.abstract: Dyslexia is a common neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent difficulties in reading and spelling. Although social and emotional challenges have been reported in individuals with dyslexia, the genetic relationships between dyslexia, social functioning, and well-being remain poorly understood. We combined phenotypic and genetic data from the Lifelines cohort with publicly available genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics. Associations between dyslexia and social traits were examined using a multi-layered approach encompassing complementary methods, including phenotypic correlation analyses, polygenic score (PGS) analyses, linkage disequilibrium score regression (LDSC), and bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR). Correlation analyses revealed significant phenotypic and genetic correlations between dyslexia and several social traits, including lower levels of life satisfaction, higher levels of loneliness, and less collegial support on the work floor. PGS analyses demonstrated that genetic liability to dyslexia predicted lower life satisfaction and reduced support from colleagues in the workplace, whereas none of the social-based PGSs predicted dyslexia. Bidirectional MR analyses provided evidence that genetic liability to dyslexia contributes to increased loneliness and social isolation, while no evidence was found for causal effects of social-interaction or well-being traits on dyslexia. Together, our results consistently supported a directional relationship from dyslexia toward social and well-being outcomes. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that dyslexia shares genetic influences with social interaction and well-being traits and suggest that genetic liability for dyslexia contributes to adverse (psycho)social outcomes. These results extend the impact of dyslexia beyond literacy-related difficulties and highlight the importance of providing social and structural support to individuals with dyslexia throughout the lifespan.

papers.title: State-independent functional connectomic architecture captures transdiagnostic network alterations and clinical variation
papers.abstract: BackgroundPsychiatric disorders show substantial overlap across diagnostic categories while differing markedly in clinical expression. Whether these shared abnormalities and individual differences are embedded in stable functional brain architecture rather than in state-specific connectivity remains unclear. MethodsWe integrated functional connectomes across one resting-state and six task-based fMRI conditions in 377 participants from the YaleNeuroConnect cohort, including 223 healthy controls and 154 individuals with psychiatric disorders. Principal component analysis was applied to each participant s functional connectivity data across the seven states to derive a state-independent connectivity representation. Network-based statistics then identified components showing significant case-control differences. Cross-state consistency was assessed, and findings were validated in an independent UCLA cohort of 177 participants. Associations between component expression and clinical measures were further examined within the Yale psychiatric group. ResultsCross-paradigm connectivity revealed two reproducible patterns of state-independent network alteration. One pattern showed reduced connectivity among limbic, somatomotor and salience systems, whereas the other showed stronger cerebellar coupling with limbic and somatomotor systems. Both patterns showed consistent case-control differences across functional states and generalized to an independent UCLA cohort. Their clinical relevance, however, differed. Greater expression of the cerebello-cortical connectivity pattern was associated with lower positive affect, greater psychopathology and more everyday executive difficulties, whereas the reduced limbic-somatomotor-salience connectivity pattern showed no significant clinical associations. ConclusionsThese findings delineate a stable reorganization of large-scale functional architecture across psychiatric disorders and suggest that broadly expressed psychiatric abnormalities and individual clinical variation may be differentially represented within the altered connectome.

papers.title: Frontoparietal functional connectivity underlies top-down attention in mild cognitive impairment
papers.abstract: BackgroundPatients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment frequently show attention problems such as reduced top-down control, the ability to ignore task-irrelevant information. It is unclear whether this reduction corresponds with decreased brain connectivity. We aimed to determine whether and how differences in functional connectivity, or the correlated activity between brain areas, explain differences in top-down control in amnestic mild cognitive impairment. MethodsWe conducted a case-control study with 26 patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (58-91 years; 10 women) and 29 age-matched healthy older adults (60-79 years; 9 women). All patients and control participants underwent neuropsychological assessment to confirm diagnosis and healthy cognitive status, respectively. We used resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging at 3T to analyse functional connectivity. Top-down control was estimated with a theory of visual attention-based verbal partial-report task (parameter ; higher indicates poorer control). We identified visual and attention-relevant functional brain networks and tested for differences between patients and controls while controlling for age and gender. ResultsCompared with healthy control participants, patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment showed lower functional connectivity in the left frontoparietal attention network and in one visual network and worse top-down control (t(37.43) = -2.24, p = 0.031). The reduced connectivity in the frontoparietal network, but not the visual network, significantly correlated with top-down control across all participants ({rho} = -0.33, p = 0.003) and in the patient group ({rho} = -0.48, p = 0.014). Moreover, connectivity in the frontoparietal network mediated the relationship between amnestic mild cognitive impairment and top-down control . DiscussionThese results link lower frontoparietal connectivity to worse attentional control in patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment. Worse control reflects inefficient attentional selection and increasing distraction by irrelevant information during perceptual processing and encoding into working memory. Overall, this implicates a role for the frontoparietal network in maintaining cognitive control or, more generally, supporting cognitive functioning in older adults with emerging cognitive impairment.

papers.title: Evidence For Clinical Utility of a Dimensional Measure of Autistic Traits in Toddlers
papers.abstract: ObjectiveThe Video-Referenced Rating of Reciprocal Social Behavior (vrRSB), a parent-report metric of quantitative autistic traits (QATs) in toddlers, leverages an innovative video scoring anchor to reliably measure heritable, continuous variation in autistic traits within the general population. However, the vrRSBs ability to distinguish toddlers with and without autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has not been formally tested. Here we compared vrRSB scores in children with and without ASD in two samples: a community-ascertained research sample (RS) recruiting toddlers with and without ASD and a clinically referred sample (CS) consisting of toddlers with concerns for ASD. MethodsT-tests and logistic regression indexed differences in vrRSB scores for toddlers with versus without ASD in both samples (RS: nASD=92, nnon-ASD=456; CS: nASD=127, nnon-ASD=44). Regression models additionally tested for differential functioning of the vrRSB relative to sex and race. ROC analysis compared classification performance of the vrRSB versus the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT). ResultsAutistic toddlers exhibited significantly higher vrRSB scores in both samples: Cohens dRS=3.68; Cohens dCS=1.04, ps .293). The vrRSB exhibited similar area under the curve as the M-CHAT in both samples and higher sensitivity in the CS. ConclusionToddler QATs show predictive validity for autism diagnostic outcome. Consistent performance across sex and racial groups suggests promise for generalizable clinical interpretation and implementation. High sensitivity of the vrRSB supports utility for secondary screening in specialty evaluations. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the National Institutes of Health. This manuscript was also supported by National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH; R01MH100027 &T32 MH100019-09).

papers.title: Prevalence and Sociodemographic Correlates of Depression and Thoughts of Self-Harm Among Adolescents in Five Low- and Middle-Income Countries: Evidence from the Demographic and Health Survey Program
papers.abstract: BackgroundAdolescence is a critical period for the onset of depression and self-harm, yet comparable, nationally representative estimates from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) remain scarce. Existing evidence relies heavily on school-based samples, excluding out-of-school adolescents. The recently available data from Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) Mental Health Module offers an opportunity to address this gap. Methods and findingsWe analysed data from 16,269 adolescents aged 15-19 years across five DHS surveys: Bangladesh (2022), Lesotho (2023-24), Mozambique (2022-23), Nepal (2022), and Zambia (2024). Probable depression was defined as a PHQ-9 score [≥]10, and thoughts of death or self-harm as any endorsement of PHQ-9 item 9. We estimated survey-weighted prevalence by country, sex, and age, examined symptom profiles, and used sex- and country-specific modified Poisson regression to identify sociodemographic correlates. The country-normalised pooled prevalence was 3.9% (95% CI 3.4-4.5) for probable depression, ranging from 0.6% in Zambia to 6.5% in Mozambique, and 7.0% (95% CI 6.4-7.7) for thoughts of death or self-harm, ranging from 3.1% to 10.2%, respectively. Girls had higher prevalence than boys for both depression (4.9% vs 1.9%) and thoughts of death or self-harm (8.6% vs 3.9%), although sex differences varied across countries. No consistent age gradient emerged. Associations with household composition, marital and parental status, urban residence, education, and wealth were heterogeneous across settings. Interpretation is limited by the lack of population-specific PHQ-9 validation and cross-country measurement invariance testing, the inability of item 9 to distinguish passive death wishes from suicidal ideation, the restriction to ever-married girls in Bangladesh, and the cross-sectional design. ConclusionsAcross five LMICs, PHQ-9-defined probable depression was relatively uncommon, while thoughts of death or self-harm affected approximately one in fourteen adolescents, particularly in girls. Substantial cross-country variation highlights the need for context-sensitive adolescent mental health surveillance and prevention, including out-of-school populations, supported by repeated household surveys and locally validated measures. Author summaryWhy was this study done? O_LIDepression and self-harm often begin during adolescence, and suicide is one of the leading causes of death among young people worldwide. C_LIO_LIIn low- and middle-income countries, most of what we know comes from school-based or local studies that use different questionnaires. These studies miss adolescents who are not in school and are hard to compare across countries. C_LIO_LIThe Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) Program recently added a mental health module to its national household surveys. This allows comparable estimates across countries for the first time. C_LI What did the researchers do and find? O_LIWe analysed responses from 16,269 adolescents aged 15-19 years in national household surveys from Bangladesh, Lesotho, Mozambique, Nepal and Zambia. All five surveys used the same questionnaire (PHQ-9) to assess depressive symptoms including suicide ideation and self-harm. C_LIO_LIAbout 4 in 100 adolescents had probable depression, ranging from under 1% in Zambia to 6.5% in Mozambique. Thoughts of death or self-harm were more common, affecting about 7 in 100 adolescents, and were more frequent than probable depression in every country. C_LIO_LIGirls reported more symptoms than boys in all countries, but the size of this gap varied widely between countries. Age, place of residence, education, wealth, marriage and parenthood showed no consistent pattern across countries. C_LI What do these findings mean? O_LIMany adolescents in these countries have thoughts of death or self-harm, including some who do not meet the threshold for probable depression. Overall, girls report higher rates than boys. Screening based only on depression scores may miss them. C_LIO_LIRisk factors differ between countries, so prevention and services should be designed for each local context. They should also reach adolescents who are not in school. C_LI

papers.title: Understanding How the Self-Regulation in Sport Practice Survey is Received by Mental Performance Consultants for Prospective Use in Applied Practice
papers.abstract: This study explored Mental Performance Consultants (MPCs) perspectives on the prospective use of the Self-Regulation in Sport Practice (SRSP) survey when consulting adolescent athletes. Twelve Canadian MPCs completed mock SRSP surveys and interviews about the surveys content and what they anticipated they could gain by using it with clients. Most of the MPCs claimed they could use the SRSP as an applied consulting resource. They believed that the SRSP could benefit the self-awareness of athletes and serve their information-gathering during case conceptualization. Most MPCs foresaw framing and enlarging SRSP statements/scores in joint discussion with a client, as part of triangulation, with some valuing the survey metrics for athletes and oneself. However, MPCs were philosophically divided on survey use, exposing uncertainty and negative preconceptions for some around quantitative assessment.

papers.title: Examining the Etiological Specificity of Genetic Risk for Alcohol Use Disorder and Alcohol Consumption through Symptom-Level Mediation Analyses
papers.abstract: IntroductionPolygenic scores (PGSs) for alcohol use disorder (AUD) may capture genetic liability related to alcohol consumption as well as broader transdiagnostic traits, including impulsivity, aggression, and neuroticism. However, the extent to which these traits account for associations between an AUD PGS and the presentation of AUD symptoms remains unclear. Thus, to better understand the genetic influences captured by an AUD PGS, the present study used mediation analyses to examine whether these transdiagnostic traits differentially mediate the relations between PGSs for AUD and individual AUD symptoms while conducting a parallel analysis using a PGS of alcohol consumption to examine differences in the genetic influences underlying AUD and consumption. MethodParticipants were drawn from the UCSF Family Alcoholism Study. Separate mediation models examined maximum habitual drinks (N = 1,611) and MMPI-2 Personality Psychopathology Five (PSY-5) scales (N = 1,464) as mediators of the association between AUD/alcohol consumption PGSs and individual AUD symptoms. Covariates included sex, age, and 10 ancestry principal components. Observations were modeled as clustered within families, and a Bonferroni correction was applied (p < .0045). ResultsRelations between the AUD PGS and AUD symptoms were fully mediated by maximum habitual drinks and partially mediated by neuroticism for nearly all symptoms, but not by other PSY-5 scales. Relations between the alcohol consumption PGS and AUD symptoms were fully mediated by maximum habitual drinks alone, with no mediation observed through any personality psychopathology measure. DiscussionCurrent AUD and alcohol consumption PGSs appear to capture genetic liability that operates predominantly through alcohol consumption. However, the AUD PGS may capture genetic influences on broader transdiagnostic factors as well, with neuroticism acting as a partial mediator. Thus, etiological interpretations of the AUD PGS as solely a measure of AUD risk should be made cautiously.

papers.title: Exploratory Symptom Profiles and Clinical Correlates in Adults with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Retrospective Study Using the Wender-Reimherr Adult Attention Deficit Disorder Scale
papers.abstract: BackgroundEmotional dysregulation (ED) is a clinically relevant feature of adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), but its relationship to clinical burden remains incompletely characterized. We aimed to describe latent symptom profiles and compare clinical and sociodemographic characteristics of adults assigned to classes with elevated probabilities in emotion-related domains with those assigned to the remaining classes. MethodsThis retrospective cross-sectional study included 749 adults with ADHD from a specialized outpatient clinic. Latent class analysis was performed on 28 items of the clinician-rated Wender-Reimherr Adult Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (WRAADDS). Classes with elevated probabilities in temper, affective lability, and emotional overreactivity were grouped post hoc as an exploratory ADHD+ED group; the remaining classes formed the ADHD group. These labels do not denote clinical diagnoses. Sensitivity analyses examined alternative groupings and adjustment for core ADHD symptom severity. ResultsA six-class solution was retained. Under the primary grouping, 60.9% of participants were assigned to ED-related classes (24.6%-77.0% across alternative groupings). The ADHD+ED group showed greater psychological distress, depressive symptoms, and functional impairment; these differences persisted after adjustment for core symptom severity. Differences on several subscales of the Conners Adult ADHD Rating Scales (CAARS) also remained, whereas differences in broader ADHD self-report scores and the number of comorbid diagnoses did not. The small difference in drug-use screening scores was not robust in sensitivity analyses; alcohol-use screening scores and sociodemographic characteristics did not differ significantly. ConclusionsAssignment to the exploratory ED-related group was associated with greater psychological distress, depressive symptoms, and functional impairment. The proportion assigned depended on the grouping and should not be interpreted as an ED prevalence estimate. The cross-sectional design limits causal inference; the single-center sample and exclusion of severe psychiatric comorbidities limit generalizability; and the shared WRAADDS basis limits independent interpretation of WRAADDS-derived group differences. Future research should use independent, dimensional measures of ED and longitudinal designs, and should evaluate interventions targeting emotion regulation in adults with ADHD.

papers.title: Statistical analysis plan for the feasibility trial assessing external trigeminal nerve stimulation versus sham stimulation for ADHD in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years (the eTNS4ADHD trial)
papers.abstract: BackgroundExternal trigeminal nerve stimulation (eTNS) is a non-invasive intervention being investigated as a potential treatment for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children and adolescents. The eTNS4ADHD trial aims to assess the feasibility of conducting a larger randomised clinical trial comparing active eTNS with sham stimulation. This paper presents the prespecified statistical analysis plan for the trial. MethodsThe eTNS4ADHD trial is a multicentre, parallel-group, randomised pilot and feasibility trial involving children and adolescents aged 7-17 years with ADHD. Participants are allocated to four weeks of active eTNS or sham stimulation. Feasibility outcomes include recruitment, treatment compliance, acceptability, follow-up completion, and concomitant treatment use. Exploratory clinical outcomes include ADHD symptoms, school absence, emotional lability, functional impairment, quality of life, sleep quality, and adverse events. All analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle. Feasibility outcomes will primarily be assessed using proportions with 95% confidence intervals, while exploratory clinical outcomes will be analysed using regression models or non-parametric methods, as appropriate. Two independent statisticians blinded to treatment allocation will conduct the analyses, and blinded conclusions will be prepared before unblinding. DiscussionThis statistical analysis plan was finalised before unblinding to promote transparency and minimise the risk of selective analyses and reporting. Given the feasibility design and limited statistical power, exploratory clinical findings will be considered hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. The results will inform the feasibility, outcome selection, sample size estimation, and statistical methodology of a future definitive randomised clinical trial evaluating eTNS for ADHD in children and adolescents. Trial registrationClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06655610.

papers.title: Maintaining EHR-based Predictive Clinical Decision Support in Mental Health against Temporal Shifts
papers.abstract: Electronic health record (EHR)-based risk prediction offers opportunities for early intervention in mental health, but models may remain in use as patient populations, care practices, and documentation change. Such temporal shifts can reduce predictive performance, while updating models from recent data alone may be unstable when adverse outcomes are uncommon. We developed Adversarial Drift-Aware Predictive Transfer (ADAPT), a distributionally robust approach to improve the temporal durability of mental health risk prediction. ADAPT uses variation in models estimated from previous calendar periods to characterize plausible changes in predictor-outcome relationships. Data from the current period constrain which historical patterns remain relevant, allowing the method to seek robustness against subsequent shifts while preserving contemporary discrimination. We retrospectively evaluated ADAPT using EHRs from 889,445 patients with mental health diagnoses at Mass General Brigham and Duke University Health System, covering one-year risk prediction for 28 outcomes. In the worst 20% of year-pair comparisons, ADAPT improved AUC over all comparators by 0.016-0.036 at Mass General Brigham, 0.011-0.018 at Duke, and 0.008-0.037 after transport. For suicide-attempt prediction, contemporary AUC at Mass General Brigham was 0.82 compared with 0.80 for the best comparator. Eight-year relative AUC degradation was 7.7%, compared with 12.1% for pooled-data training. These results suggest that information from prior temporal shifts can improve robustness to future changes without sacrificing predictive performance for current patients.
